OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. members, I refer with profound sorrow to the pass-
ing away of Shri Abu Abraham, a form er Member of the Rajya Sabha on the 
1" December, 2002 at the age of 78 years. 
Bom at Thiruvalla in Kerala in June, 1924, Shri Abu Abraham had his educa-
tion at the University College, Trivandrum. A journalist and cartoonist by pro-
fession, Shri Abraham was associated with several newspapers and journals. 
He started his career as a reporter of the Bombay Chronicle and later joined the 
Shankers' Weekly, New Delhi, in 1951. He was the only Indian cartoonist who 
worked in England for The Guardian and The Observer for 16 years as a political 
cartoonist. His cartoons earned him much popularity. He had many publications 
on cartoons to his credit. 
Shri Abu Abraham was a nominated Member of the Rajya Sabha from April. 
1972 to April, 1978. 
In the passing away of Shri Abu Abraham, the country has lost an eminent 
journalist and a noted cartoonist. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Abu Abraham. 
I request the Members to rise in thei r places and observe silence for one 
minute as a mark of respect to the memory of the departed soul. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for one minute.) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: The Secretary-General will convey to the members of the 
bereaved family our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Expenditure on health care 
* 181. PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the expenditure on health care in 
percentage of GDP has been declining, whereas health care needs have grown j|^ 
steadily over the years; and ^ 
(b) the steps taken to raise the Central and State health outlays appropriately 
in view of the emerging new challenges to health and to ensure adequate health 
care facilities in all parts of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI 
SHATRUGHAN SINHA): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) As per World Health Report, 2002 of WHO, the percentage of total 
expenditure on health to GDP has remained in the vicinity of 5% since 1995. 
The health care needs over the years have no doubt grown with the increase in 
population, 
(b) Government has been making every ef fort to increase its contribution 
to public health expenditure. The resources for public investment in health 
sector are being augiTiented by securing assistance from various bilateral and 
multilateral agencies for implementation of various disease control 
programmes. To provide quality health care services to the people in the rural 
areas, especially the poor and the underserved, health infrastructure is being 
upgraded under the State Health Syst ems Project which is presently under 
implementation In seven States with World Bank assistance. The project will 
be gradually extended to other States. Additional Central Assistance is provided 
to States/UTs under the Prime Minister Gramodaya Yojana as well. 
The National Health Policy—2002 announced by the Government during 
the year envisages increasing public health investment to 2% of GDP by the 
year 2010 from the.existing 0.9%. It is also proposed in the Policy that State 
Governments would increase their expenditure on health sectors to 7% of their 
total budget by 2005 and to 8% of the budget by 2010. The Central 
Government contribution would rise to 25% from the existing 15% by 2010. 
Government is making all efforts to increase expenditure on health as per the 
Policy subject to overall financial constraints, The Tenth Plan outlay for Central 
Health Sector subject to approval (by National Development Council) has been 
fixed at Rs. 9253 crore compared to Rs. 5118 crore during the Ninth Plan.

AIDS/HIV among the age group of 12— 25 
*I82. SHRI LAJPAT RAI: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) the estimated number of AIDS/HIV positive women and men in the age 
group of 12-25 as on 1" January, 2000 in the country; 
(b) the number of deaths because of this disease during the past three years, 
year-wise. State-wise; and 
(c) the steps taken to minimise the casualities and the results thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI 
SHATRUGHAN SfNH A): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the table of the House. 
Statement 
The National AIDS Control Organization, Government of India conducts 
Nation wide HIV Sentinel Surveillance every year during the period August-
October, covering both high-risk groups as well as general population. This 
data is also used to estimate the burden of HIV infections in the country in the 
adult population between 15-49 years of age group by taking certain assump-

tions into consideration. However, disaggregated HIV estimates in various age 
groups are not made. Based on the HIV Sentinel Surveillance data from 1999, 
estimate of 3.7 million HIV infections was made, which include 2.2 million 
i n f e c t i o n s  a m o n g  m e n  a n d   1 . 5  million i n f e c t i o n s  a m o n g  w o m e n .  
The estimated number of HIV infections in the year 1998 was 3.5 million, 
1999 as 3.7 million, 2000 as 3.86 million and 2001 as 3.97 million infections. 
These estimates indicate that there has not been much upsurge in the spread 
of HIV infection in the country. 
As per reports received from States/UTs in the country, 1372 AIDS deaths 
have been reported to National AIDS Control Organisation during last three 
years. A Statement (Statement-I) indica ting number of deaths State-wise and 
year-wise during each of last three years is annexed. (See below). 
Government of India is implementing a Nation-wide comprehensive National 
AIDS Control Programme through autonomous AIDS Control Societies at State, 
UT and Municipal levels. The main components of the programme are:- 
(i) Reducing the HIV transmission amongst poor and marginalized sec-
tions of the community at the high risk of infection, by (a) targeted 
interventions amongst marginalized sections of the society at the h igh-
est risk of HIV infection and transmission such as sex workers, trans-
port work TS, injecting drug users, men who have sex with men, m igrant 
workers, industrial workers vulnerable to HIV infection, street children 
and slum population; (b) control of sexually transmitted diseases 
through syndromic management at the peripheral public health institu-
tions and through outreach services; and (c) condom promotion to 
prevent the sexual transmission of HIV; 
(ii) Reducing the spread of HIV amongst general population, which is 
perceived to be at a lower risk; by (a) reducing blood based transmis-
sion by modernizing the blood transfusion services in the country for 
greater availability and rational use of blood, by ensuring mandatory 
screening of HIV, Hepatitis 'B' and 'C, malaria and syphilis and by 
developing technical manpower; (b) Information, Education and Com-
munication campaigns to raise awareness levels; and (c) promotion of 
voluntary counseling and testing for HIV; 
(iii) Strengthen the institutions responsible for implementation of the 
programme, by—(a) increasing the quantity, quality and timeliness 
of surveillance systems for HIV, sexually transmitted infections, 
behaviour patterns and social determinants in all parts of the country

(iv) Delivery of community based low cost care for people living with

and Nagaland; and (d) encouraging people living with HlV/AlDS to

(v) Ensuring multisectoral collaboration with public, private and voluntary 
sectors for a broad based response to  the epidemic. At present, over 
700 targeted intervention projects in the country are being run through 
Non-Government Organisations. Besides, NGOs are being involved 
in running community care centres and school AIDS education 
programme. 
The various ministries/departments like Defence, Railways, Labour,

Social Justice and Empowerment are implementing HIV/AIDS pre-

Statement 
The measures adpoted to control population by the Government have yielded 
favourable results, the Total Fertility Rate has come down from 6in 1951 to3.2 
in 1999. The Birth Rate has come down from 40.8 in 1951 to 25.8 during the year 
2000. as per the estimates of Sample Registration System (SRS), Registrar General 
of India. According to National Family Health Survey conducted in 1998-99, 
42% ofthe couples with two children and about 58% of couples with 3 children 
have adopted terminal methods of contraception. The child population (0—6 
yeai^) has come down from 18% in 1991 to 15% in 2001 census, showing decline 
in fertility rate. 
Among the major States with more than 20 million population, the States of 
Kerala and Tamil Nadu have already achieved a replacement level of fertility of a 
TFR of 2.1, while the States of Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat. Karnataka, Maharashtra, 
Orissa, Punjab and West Bengal are having a TFR of 2.2 to 3.0 and are in the 
direction ofreplacement level of fertility. There are 4 States v/r. Assam, Madhya 
Pradesh, Chhattisgarh and Haryana which are having a TFR of 3.1 to 4.0, while 
the 4 States of Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Jharkhand have recorded a 
TFR of 4.1 to 4.7 as per the SRS, 1999. 
Regarding the acceptance of terminal methods, the percentage of couples 
with two children have high acceptance in Southern and Western regipns, being 
60% in Tamil Nadu, 72% in^ndhra Pradesh, 50% in Maharashtra and 60% in

*199. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND

annexed at Statement I to III (See below). Health being a State subject under the 
Constitution of India, it is the responsibility of the respective State to provide 
necessary health care facilities in their Government hospitals according to the 
need and resources available with th em. The Central Government, however, 
apart from the assistance given under various Centrally sponsored schemes, 
also support the State Governments for upgrading secondary health care system 
with the World Bank assistance under State Health System Projects. So far as 
Central Government Hospitals are concerned, sufficient health care facilities are 
available there. Improvement/upgradation of health care facilities in the Central 
Government Hospitals is a continuous  process and necessary measures are 
being taken in view of the advancement of medical science and available 
resources.

1197. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news-item 
captioned "Darjeeling in Act will help Tea Industry", which appeared in the 
Asian Age, dated the 10th October, 2002; 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto; and 
(c) the steps proposed to address the problem highlighted in the news-
item, so as to assist the ailing Tea Indu stry to compete with neighbouring tea 
producing countries like Sri Lanka and Nepal? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Government 
has initiated action to protect Darjeeling tea under various legal frameworks 
that exist in different importing countries. The Darjeeling tea logo is registered 
in various countries including UK, Germany, Italy, Switzerland, Belgium, 
Netherlands, Portugal, USA, Japan, Egypt and Canada. The Darjeeling tea 
word and logo are registered as a Certification Trade Mark in India and would 
also be registered under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration 
and Protection) Act 1999, once it is operationalised. 
(c) While Sri Lankan tea is not similar in character to Darjeeling tea and 
hence does not pose a direct competition vis-a-vis the requirements of the 
Darjeeling tea in export markets, Nepal tea poses a competitive challenge to 
Darjeeling tea. The agro-climauc condition, under which Nepal teas are grown, 
is closer to that of Darjeeling with the added advantage of newer bushes. 
Darjeeling tea, however, has greater brand value and image and the Government 
has taken action to protect the brand name legally as well as implement a 
monitoring system that will address the problem of alleged misuse.

Export Credit, higher moratorium period and simpler norms for fresh loans for 
the Coffee growers;

age? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI RAJIV PRATAP RUDI): (a) and (b) Concerned with the prob-
lems of the coffee growers, who are facing hardships due to prevailing low 
prices, the Government of India have taken a series of steps in the recent 
months for the benefit of the coffee sector. This includes a special relief pack-
age for the coffee growers (announced by the Reserve Bank of India) under 
which the term loans as well as crop loans of the Banks have been consolidated 
into a Special Coffee Term Loan (SCTL) with repayment period of 9-11 years 
and repayment holiday of 3 years. The package includes grant of fresh loans, 
reduction of interest rate on SCTL by 1 %, deferment of interest due on SCTL 
during the current year to be recovered over the next 3 years etc. In addition, 
the Government of India is also providing 5% interest relief to small growers on 
the working capital loans taken by them from financial institutions, besides a 
package of incentives for export of coffee and implementing innovative market-
ing strategies in the international as well as domestic markets to arrest the 
decline in exports and also to increase domestic consumption etc. Further, the 
Tenth Five Year Plan programmes and schemes of the Coffee board have been 
formulated to ensure long-term devel opment of the sector. Recently, on the 
advice of the Government, the National Bank for Agricultural and Rural Devel-
opment (NABARDJ has also set up a "Plantation Industry Cell", for providing 
prompt attention to the credit related problems of the plantation industry. 
As regards liberal export credit, the general concessions available to the 
exporters such as availab ility of credit at concessional rate of interest from 
bsnks in respect of pre-shipment and post-shipment advances to exporters are 
available to coffee exporters also.

SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA:

(a) whether Government are aware of the contents of US-based National

90 

[2 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) the reaction of Government on the controversy cover the number of 
AIDS affected people in the country; 
(c) the number of people died due to AI DS during the last three years and 
the estimated   number of infected people in the country; 
(d) anti-AlDS programmes of Government against spread of the disease; and 
(e) whether Government find any vested interest behind the ill-advised 
report and the recently announced 100 million dollar grant by a foreign 
foundation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b ) The recent repon of the National 
Intelligence Council (NIC) states that the number of people with HIV/AIDS 
will grow significantly by the end of the decade. The increase will be driven 
by the spread of the disease in five populous countries: Nigeria. Ethiopia. 
Russia, India and China, where the number of infected people will grow from 
around 14 to 23 million currently to an estimated 50 to 75 million by 2010. 
It is reported that the HIV/AIDS is spreading at different rates in the five 
countries, with the epidemic being most advanced in Nigeria and Ethiopia. 
The official adult prevalence rate is al most 6 per cent in Nigeria, between 10 
and 18 per cent in Ethiopia, around I to 2 per cent in Russia, around I per cent 
in India and 0.15 to 0.25 per cent in China. Heterosexual transmission of the 
HIV virus is the primary mode to spread In Nigeria, Ethiopia and India- 
while Intravenous drug use drives the spread of the disease in Russia. Several 
factors are driving the epidemic in China — the large migrant population, 
Intravenous drug users and poor hygiene in plasma sales. 
The National AIDS Control Organisation, Government of India conducts 
Nation wide HIV Sentinel Surveillance every year during the period 
August—October. This data is also used to estimate the burden of HIV 
infections in the country in the adults population between 15— 49 years of 
age group by taking certain assumptions into consideration. Based on the HIV 
Sentinel Surveillance data from 2001, estimate of 3.9? million HIV infections 
was made. As such, Government does not agree with the NIC (National 
Intelligence Council) report. 
(c) 1372 deaths due to AIDS have been reported to National AIDS Control 
Organisation during last three years. Based on annual round of HIV Sentinel 
surveillance 2001, it is estimated that th ere are 3.97 million HIV infections in 
the country. 
91 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2002] 
(d) The Government of India is implementing Second Phase of the National 
AIDS Control Programme which has two key objectives: 
(1) To reduce the spread of HIV infection in India; and (2) to strengthen 
India's capacity to respond to HIV/AIDS on a long term basis. 
The programme has five distinct components with specific strategies under 
each of them. 
(i) Reducing the HIV transmission amongst poor and marginalized 
sections of the community at the high risk of infection, by (a) 
targeted interventions amongst marginalized sections of the society 
at the highest risk of HIV infection and transmission such as sex 
workers, transport workers, injecting drug users, men who have

Cosmetics Act and Rules made thereunder. 
The evaluation of new drug applications is a complex process as per 
Schedule-V under Drugs and Cosmetics rules and varies according to the 
nature of molecule/drug, published data and information furnished by the 
applicants. Therefore, depending upon the nature of the application, it may 
take on an average 3 to 5 years for an applicant to complete all phase of trials 
required for approval of investigational New Drug {i.e. a drug molecule not 
tested on human being anywhere in th e world); about 1—3 years for the first 
time approval of the drug already approved elsewhere but requiring confirma-
tory clinical trial, and about 2-3 months for subsequent applications for al-
ready approved drugs. This is however, subject to submission of all required 
data as per provisions of Schedule-Y of Drug and Cosmetics Rules and opin-
ion from experts. Certain critical drugs e.g. anti-cancer, anti-HIV, immuno-
suppresent, etc., which are critical from the point of view of public health are 
cleared on a fast track basis.

National Testing Policy on HIV 
1275. DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there are any regulations to monitor the implementation of the 
norms of National Testing Policy on HIV; 
123 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2002] 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the provisions to check flouting of the norms? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) Government of India has approved the 
National AIDS Prevention and Control Policy in April, 2002 which clearly 
states that there is no public health rational for mandatory testing of a person 
for HIV/AIDS. HIV testing should be carried out on a voluntary basis with 
appropriate pre-test and post-test counselling. These guidelines have been 
circulated to all State Governments for implementation. The statement in this 
regard is given below: 
Statement 
The details and the provisions to check flouting of the norms are in the "para 
5.6" of "National AIDS Prevention and Control Policy" 
"5.6 my testing 
5.6.1 There is an active debate in the country on the issue of mandatory 
testing of people suspected of carrying HIV infection. Considerable thought 
has been given to this issue. The Government feels that there is no public 
health rationale for mandatory testing of a person for HIV/AIDS. On the other 
hand, such an approach could be coun ter-productive as it  may scare away a 
large number of suspected cases from getting detected and treated. HIV testing 
carried out on a voluntary basis with appropriate pre-test and post-test 
counselling is considered to be a better strategy and is in line with the WHO 
guidelines on HIV testing. Government of India has earlier issued a comprehensive 
HIV testing policy and the following issues are reiterated here:- 
(I) No individual should be made to undergo a mandatory testing for HIV. 
(ii) No mandatory HIV testing shoul d be imposed as a precondition for 
employment or for providing health care facilities during employment. 
However, in the case of Armed Forces, before employment, HIV 
screening may be carried out voluntarily with pretest and post-test 
counselling and the results may be kept confidential. 
(iii) Adequate voluntary testing fac ilities with pre-test and post-test 
counselling should be made available throughout the country in a 
phased manner. There should be at least one HIV testing centre in 
each district in the country with proper counselling facilities. 
(iv) In case a person likes to get the HIV status verified through testing, all 
necessary facilities should be given to that person and results 
124 

[2 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
should be kept strictly confidential. Such results should be given out 
to the person and with his consent to the members of his family. 
Disclosure of the HIV status to the spouse or sexual partner of the 
person should invariably be done by the attending physician with 
proper counselling. However, the person should also be encouraged 
to share this information with the family for getting proper home-
based care and emotional support from the family members. 
(v) In case of marriage, if one of the pa rtners insists on a test to check the 
HIV status of the other partner; such tests should be carried out by the 
contracting party to the satisfaction of the person concerned. 
5.6.2. The HIV testing policy adopted is found to be appropriate for different 
types of testing done under the programme. At present people are tested for- 
(a) Screening in blood banks 
(b) epidemiological surveys; and 
(c) confirmatory testing for clinical management and voluntary testing. 
In the case of screening for blood donation, a single test of ERS (ELISA/ 
Rapid/Simple) is conducted to eliminate HIV sero-reactive blood. In the case 
of epidemiological surveys, two tests either with ELISA, or Rapid or Simple 
will be done. In both these cases the testing is unlinked and anonymous. In 
the case of diagnosis of clinically su spected cases and for voluntary testing, 
the testing will be done with 3 ERS us ing HIV kits with different antigens. 
HIV testing under these conditions will be carried out with proper pre-testing 
and post-testing counselling with informed consent of the individual and with 
proper follow up facilities. 
5.6.3 in case of HIV testing facilities in the private sector hospitals, clinics, 
nursing homes and diagnostic centres, the State Governments should adopt 
legislative and other measures to ensure  that these testing centres conform to 
the national policy and guidelines relating to HIV testing."

Industry status to film industry 
1295. SHRI SANJAY NIRUPAM: Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether her Ministry has accorded the status of industry to the film 
144 

[2 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
industry in the country; 
(b) if so, the special arrangements and provisions given to film producers 
to give them finanical support; 
(c) whether corporate funding of Indian films has happened after that; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) Yes Sir. 
(b) to (d) Under the Industrial Bank of India (IDBI) Act, 1964 Section 2(c) (xvii) 
"Entertainment Industry including films" has been included as an 'approved 
activity' under 'industrial concern'. Both IDBI as well as RBI have formulated 
schemes/guidelines specifically for financing production of films by financial 
institutions and public sector banks respectively. 
As per RBI guidelines, Public Sector Banks may finance production of films 
of producers with good track record subject to certain conditions. The RBI 
guidelines state that ordinarily producers are required to bring in at least 25 per 
cent of the project cost as promoters contribution and also tie up with the 
distributors and receive advances as per usual practices to cover 35 per cent to 
40 per cent of the budget. It has thus been stipulated in the guidelines that bank 
advances would be for the balance requirement of 35 to 40 per cent of the cost. 
However, in deserving cases where the Banks are quite comfortable with the 
project as well as the background of the producers, the financing can be in-
creased upto 50 per cent of the project cost on merits. 
Under IDBI's scheme financial institutions are to initially focus on financing 
film production activity of corporate entities. While there is no upper hmit for 
sanction, the minimum quantum of assistance would normally be not less than 
Rs. 20 million. The quantum of assistance would not exceed 50 per cent of the 
budget, the debt—equity ratio would not exceed 1:1 and the promoter's contri-
bution has to be at least 30 per cent of the estimated budget and can be raised in 
the form of advances from distributors against sale of territories music/video 
rights etc. The period of repayment of loan would not exceed two years and 
loans would be sanctioned against various forms of securities specified in the 
scheme. 
Information regarding lending by public sector banks is not centrally main-
tained. According to reports received from IDBI during the year 2001-02, 
145 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December, 2002] 
IDBI had allocated Rs. 100 crore for the scheme of financing film production and 
disbursements have been made to the tune of Rs. 40.10 crores till the period 
ending August 2002.

Adoption of Court Management Techniques 
1306. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRI GIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are laying emphasis on adoption of Court 
Management techniques by the subordinate courts for reducing the huge 
backlog of pending cases; and 
(b) if so, the details of the Court Management techniques? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI K. JANA 
KRISHNAMURTHY): (a) and (b) The su bordinate Judiciary is under the 
control of the concerned High Courts. It is primary responsibility of the High 
Courts to take necessary action regarding Court Management in consultation 
with the respective State Governments.  However the Supreme Court of India 
has taken a number of measures to redu ce the pendency in the Supreme Court 
which, inter-alia, include the following:— 
(i)   More practical categorization & grouping of cases 
(ii)   Stabilization of Benches 
(iii) As far as possible cases scheduled to be taken up for hearing on a day 
should be listed for that day. 
(iv) No accumulation of defective matters. 
(v) Reservation of more and sufficient slots for old pending Misc. and SLP 
matters, so that they are listed in  chronological order in sufficient 
numbers. 
166 

[2 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(vi) Better utilization of available computer network. 
(vil) Streamlining of administration and manpower so that there is neither 
excess nor less work at every desk, and to make constant efforts for 
improving the quality of work by the Registry staff. 
High Courts have been requested to adopt similar measures to reduce the 
pendency of cases. The High Courts have also been requested to implement 
the recommendations of the Malimath Committee to streamline procedure 
which will, inter-alia, expedite disposal of pending cases. 
The Central Government has initiated a pilot project for Computerisation 
of City Civil Courts in the four metropolises of Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and 
Kolkata at an approximate cost of Rs. 14.91 crores to serve as a model. 
An amount of Rs. 518.76 lakhs has been released during 2002-2003 for 
the use of Information Technology in courts to various States/UTs under the 
Centrally Sponsored Scheme. This will include establishment of computerised 
enquiry/facilitation centres in the high Courts.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI O RAJAGOPAL): (a) to (e) Urban 
Development Is a State subject. It is therefore, the responsibility of the States 
to ensure urban development and mobilise requisite resources for the purpose. 
However, Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation supplements 
the efforts of the State Governments through policy formulation, technical 
guidance and Central assistance under Centrally sponsored schemes. 
A Conference of Ministers of Urban Development, Local Self-Govemment 
and Housing of States/Union Territories was convened at New Delhi on 12th 
September, 2002 by the Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty 
Alleviation. The need of adopting new fiscal instruments for developing 
urban infrastructure was emphasized. New fiscal instruments included 
financing commercial urban infrastruct ure projects through  access to capital 
market, credit rating of municipal and urban infrastructure entities, forging 
public-private partnership in the provision of urban infrastructure. A final 
decision to adopt new approach would lie with the States. 
The following fiscal instruments announced in the Union Budget 2002-03 
were discussed at the conference:— 
(i) Urban Reforms Incentive Fund (URIF). 
(il) City Challenge Fund (CCF). 
(ill) Pooled Finance Development Scheme (PFDS). 
URIF has been set up to provide reform  linked assistance to States in the 
following areas:— 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [2 December. 2002] 
(i) Reform of Rent Control Laws and repeal of Urban Land Ceiling Acts. 
(ii) Rationalisation of high stamp duty regimes. 
(iii) Revision of bye-laws to streamline the approvals process for 
construction of buildings, development of sites, etc. 
(iv) Revision of municipal laws in line with model legislation prepared by 
the Ministry of Urban Development and Poverty Alleviation. 
(v) Simplification of legal and procedural frameworks for conversion of 
agricultural land for non-agriculture purposes. 
(vi) Levy of realistic user charges and resource mobilization by urban 
local bodies. 
(vii) Initiation of public private partnership in the provision of civic 
services. 
CCF is an incentive based facility that will support cities to fund 
transitional costs of moving towards sustainable and creditworthy 
institutional systems of municipal management and service delivery. It will 
assist in the partial Financing of the cost of developing an economic reform 
programme and financially viable projects to be undertaken by urban local 
bodies. 
PFDS is meant to provide credit enhancement to assist local bodies to 
access market borrowing on a creditworthy basis. 
At the conference it was further stated that in order to provide incentive 
for urban local bodies to become creditworthy and invest in urban 
infrastructure. Government has provide d for the issue of municipal tax-free 
bonds upto Rs. 500 crores in 2002-03. The States should make use of the 
provision and send suitable proposals to the Government. 
The following were the other issues discussed at the conference:—

AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI O. RAJAGOPAL): (a) World Health

[2 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Statement 
Extracts taken from guidelines For drinking water quality (Second 
Edition), Volume I Recommendations, World Health Organisation, 
Geneva 1993. 
Iron 
Iron is one of the most abundant metals in the earth's crust. It is found in 
natural fresh waters at levels ranging from 0.5 to 50 mg/litre. Iron may also be 
present in drinking water as a result of the use of iron coagulants or the 
corrosion of steel and cast iron pipes during water distribution. 
Iron Is an essential element in human nutrition. Estimates of minimum 
daily requirement for iron depend on age, sex, physiological status, and iron 
bio-availability and range from about 10 to 50 mg/day. 
As a precaution-against storage in the body of excessive iron, in 1983, 
JECFA established a provisional maximum tolerable daily intake (PMTDI) of 
0.8 mg/kg. of body weight, which applies to iron from all sources except for 
iron oxides used as colouring agents, and iron supplements taken during 
pregnancy and lactation or for specific clinical requirements. An allocation of 
10% of this PMTDI to drinking water gives a value of about 2 mg/litre which 
does not present a hazard to health. The taste and appearance of drinking 
water will usually be affected below this level. 
Anaerobic ground water may contain ferrous iron at concentration of upto 
several milligrams per litre without discoloration or turbidity in water when 
directly pumped from a well. On exposure to the atmosphere, however, the 
ferrous iron oxidizes to ferric iron, giving an objectionable reddish-brown 
colour to the water. 
Iron also promotes the growth of "iron bacteria", which derive their energy 
from the oxidation of ferrous iron to ferriq iron and in the process deposit a 
slimy coating on the piping. 
At levels above 0.3 mg/litre. iron stains laundry and plumbing fixtures. 
There is usually no noticeable taste at iron concentrations below 0.3 mg/litre 
although turbidity and colour may develop. Iron concentrations of I—3 mg/ 
litre can be acceptable for people drinking anaerobic well-water. 
No health-based guideline value is proposed for iron.

SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I welcome the Securities 
and Exchange Board of India (Amendm ent) Bill, 2002. The Securities and 
Exchange Board of India Act, 1992 was enacted to provide for the 
establishment of a Board to protect the interests of investors in securities and 
to promote and regulate the development of securities market. 
The new amendments would definitely improve the organisational 
structure and institutional capacity. These amendments would strengthen the 
mechanisms available to the SEBI for inve stigation and enforcement so that it 
is better  equipped to investigate the malpractices. 
It is a welcome move which will definitely address the long-standing 
problems of the vibrant capital market  and will protect the interests of the 
inveslors- 
Jt has got some other striking f eatures also. Calling for information 
and record from any bank or other aut hority, or a board, or a corporation 
established or constituted by or under any Central, State or Provincial Act in 
respect of any transaction in securities which are under investigation or inquiry 
by a board, would not only protect the investors but would facilitate to have a 
vibrant market. 
314 

[2 December, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
The new amendments would give t eeth to the SEBI to direct any 
intermediary or any person associated with the securities market in any 
manner not to dispose of or alienate an asset forming part of any transaction 
which is under investigation. 
The SEBI would have powers to impose deterrent fine up to Rs. 25 
crores or three times the undue profit  derived  by connmitting offences, 
whichever is higher. 
The quantum of fine would go up from the present range of 
Rs.5.000/- to Rs. 5 lakhs and from Rs. 1 lakh to Rs. 25 crores or even more.

Consolidated Fund of India which would definitely help the exchequer. Sir, the 
other striking feature is amending the co mposition of the Securities Appellate 
Tribunal. This will help the speedy disposal of cases and facilitate easy justice 
to the investors. The bold initiative of  enhancing the penalties will definitely 
prohibit malpractices, manipulative and fraudulent trade practices and insider 
trading to the maximum extent. The majo r thrust here is that Government 
should implement the provision in lette r and spirit to further strengthen the 
mechanism of investigation and enforcem ent to protect Ehe capital market 
and interests of investors. Thank you. Sir.
